newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH '97 C/A GAP SEEN AT $6.5 BLN, 5 PCT OF GDP.
newsitem.headline: POLISH '97 C/A GAP SEEN AT $6.5 BLN, 5 PCT OF GDP.

text.p: Poland's current account gap is seen widening to $6.5 billion or five percent of gross doemstic product in 1997 against a $1.35 billion or one percent of GDP deficit in 1996, a senior government analyst said.

Zbigniew Kuzmiuk, head of the Centre for Stratgic Studies told a news conference on Wednesday the trade gap was likely to grow to $13 billion against the government's 1997 budget plan of $9.5 billion.

"This is a worrying figure," Kuzmiuk said. "The growth rate of imports is still much faster than that of exports even though European Union countries, our main export market, are just coming out of recession," he said.

Polish imports grew 24.9 percent in the first half of the year against the same period of last year to $18.18 billion while exports rose 9.2 percent to $12.46 billion bringing the trade gap to $5.72 billion against a $3.15 billion gap in 1996.

"Despite the negative trends of the first half, we expect that in the whole of 1997 exports growth will be faster than in 1996 thanks to an improving business climate in the European Union and export oportunities in the East," Kuzmiuk said.
He said the CSS expected total exports growth in 1997 at 11 percent against 1996 and imports growth at 23 percent.
"The slighly faster exports growth and slower imports are also likely to be party a result of the recent weakening of the zloty," Kuzmiuk said.

The July floods, which swamped 6,000 sq km killing 54 people and causing damage of billions of dollars, prompted large-scale zloty sales by foreign investors, concerned that flood relief spending would worsen Polish fundamentals.

Investors were especially concerned about the 2.5 billion zloty flood relief credit which parliament imposed on the independent central bank, saying it was the worst possible way of financing from the poinit of view of inflation.

The large government loan coupled with a money supply jump of 4.1 percent in July made the National Bank of Poland raise its main interest rates by two and 2.5 points to 27 and 24.5 percent respectively on August 4.

"The 4.1 percent jump in July means money supply growth is out of the NBP's control and further tightening is needed with post-flood credit outflows still ahead," Krzysztof Rybinski, chief economist at ING Bank in Warsaw, told Reuters.

Credit for households and companies rose 32 percent and 17.2 percent respectively since the start of the year until the end of July while household deposits rose only 22.4 percent and company deposits fell 0.9 percent.

Analysts said the rise of interest rates may prove not very effective against curbing credit growth amid fast rising real wages and high consumer optimism, even though it was badly needed to slow down imports.
"The problem is not with exports but with excessive growth of imports as consumer optimism is around record highs ahead of the elections," Rybinski said.
Poland is to hold parliamentary polls on September 21.

CSS' Kuzmiuk said the falling propensity to save and rising propensity to spend, especially on high quality imported goods such as new cars, was a result of an explosion of long constrained demand and optimism about future wage growth.

Gross real wages in the enterprise sector have grown 5.1 percent in the first half of the year against the same period of last year and the CSS expects that although their growth rate would slow down only sligtly in the comming months.
